articles.title: One gunshot, three executions: the Devil’s River murder of 1863
articles.summary: The murder of Robert Scott became a capital case against three people—and a record of how colonial Victoria failed to reckon with domestic violence.
articles.author: Al Zadid Yusuf

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: This history involves domestic violence, murder and execution. It is not a neat mystery story: the surviving record tells us what a colonial court decided, but it also shows how much that court left outside its frame.

sections.title: A gunshot at Devil’s River
paragraphs: Robert and Elizabeth Scott kept a remote refreshment house in the Wappan district near Mansfield. Around midnight on 11 April 1863, Robert Scott was killed by a single shotgun blast.

Police arrested Elizabeth and two men associated with the household, David Gedge and Julian Cross. The Crown’s case eventually presented the killing as a conspiracy. Forgotten Australia’s three-part *Murder at Devil’s River* series returns to the central question that still makes the case troubling: did the verdict explain what actually happened inside the shanty?

sections.title: The life the prosecution pushed aside
paragraphs: Public Record Office Victoria researcher Emma Beach reconstructed Elizabeth’s history from judicial records. At twelve, Elizabeth was sent to Goomalibee station as an indentured servant. Before she turned fourteen, the substantially older Robert Scott had acquired her contract and married her.

Beach’s archival study describes repeated domestic violence during the marriage. Yet the prosecution centred an alleged relationship between Elizabeth and Gedge as the motive for murder. Her experience of abuse was not developed by her defence as a reason to understand her conduct or mitigate her sentence. An all-male jury therefore heard a story about adultery and conspiracy, not the fuller history of coercion recorded around the case.

sections.title: Three convictions, one scaffold
paragraphs: Elizabeth Scott, David Gedge and Julian Cross were convicted of Robert Scott’s murder. A murder conviction then carried a mandatory death sentence. Public Record Office Victoria explains that the later capital-case review concerned whether mercy should commute that sentence, not whether the conviction itself was sound.
The Executive Council did not recommend mercy. On 11 November 1863, all three were executed at Melbourne Gaol. Elizabeth was 23 and became the first woman executed in the Colony of Victoria.

sections.title: Four facts that survive the uncertainty

list.label: Robert Scott was killed.
list.text: He died from a gunshot at the household’s isolated roadside business on 11 April 1863.

list.label: The colonial court convicted three people.
list.text: Elizabeth Scott, David Gedge and Julian Cross were held legally responsible and sentenced to death.

list.label: The executions followed a separate mercy process.
list.text: The capital files could determine whether a death sentence was commuted, but did not retry guilt.

list.label: Domestic violence belongs in the history.
list.text: Archival research documents sustained abuse and shows that it was not meaningfully presented in Elizabeth’s defence.

sections.title: What the record does not settle
paragraphs: The precise role of each accused remains contested in later accounts. It would be irresponsible to turn that uncertainty into a confident declaration of innocence; it would be equally misleading to treat the 1863 verdict as a complete and neutral account.

The most defensible conclusion is narrower. Robert Scott was murdered. Three people were convicted and hanged. But the process that judged Elizabeth treated her gender, marriage and alleged sexuality as more legible than the violence she had endured.

sections.title: Why this case is worth remembering
paragraphs: Forgotten Australia revived the case as a question about whether the gallows delivered justice. The archival record makes that question larger than the identity of the person who fired the weapon. It asks what justice can mean when a court recognises a violent death but fails to properly recognise the violence that came before it.

That is why the Devil’s River case should not be reduced to a macabre first—the first woman executed in Victoria—or packaged as a solved puzzle. Its value lies in the tension between verdict and history, and in the people and circumstances the official story struggled to see.

articles.title: Three steps to eight hours: Melbourne’s 1856 campaign
articles.summary: A one-minute history of how Melbourne stonemasons helped establish the eight-hour working day—and who the first victory left out.
articles.author: Al Zadid Yusuf

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: On 21 April 1856, Melbourne stonemasons stopped work and marched for an eight-hour day. The event became a landmark in Australian labour history, but the change was neither instant nor universal.

list.label: Set the date.
list.text: A public meeting at Melbourne’s Queen’s Theatre resolved that the building trades would begin working eight-hour days on 21 April.

list.label: Walk out.
list.text: Stonemasons left the University of Melbourne building site and marched towards Parliament House, gathering workers from other sites along the way.

list.label: Keep negotiating.
list.text: In the following months, an agreement gave stonemasons eight-hour days without reducing the pay they had received for ten hours.

sections.title: The part worth remembering
paragraphs: The first victory covered only a minority of workers, mainly in building trades. Victoria did not pass an Eight Hours Act until 1916, and a nationwide 40-hour, five-day week was not approved until 1948.
The campaign’s enduring idea was a day divided into equal parts: work, recreation and rest. Melbourne’s Eight Hour Monument, at Russell and Victoria streets, still records that “888” principle.

articles.title: One show, one snack, three towns: Wagga Wagga’s Chiko Roll moment
articles.summary: A one-minute history of the Chiko Roll’s documented 1951 Wagga Wagga debut—and why that does not settle where it was invented.
articles.author: Al Zadid Yusuf

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: Wagga Wagga did not simply “invent” the Chiko Roll. Its more defensible claim is just as interesting: the city hosted the snack’s documented public breakthrough.

list.label: Developed in Victoria.
list.text: Bendigo boilermaker and caterer Frank McEncroe developed a sturdier, one-handed alternative to a chop-suey roll he had seen outside a Richmond football ground.

list.label: Launched in Wagga.
list.text: The new roll appeared at the 1951 Wagga Wagga Agricultural Show. The Australian Dictionary of Biography says it was acclaimed there; Wagga Wagga City Council describes the event as its first commercial sale.

list.label: Claimed by several places.
list.text: Wagga, Bendigo and Bathurst later argued over the snack’s home. The council itself calls Wagga’s “birthplace” claim controversial and records the manufacturer’s position that the origins are varied and complex.

sections.title: What Wagga can confidently claim
paragraphs: Wagga was the launch stage, not the whole origin story. For the Chiko Roll’s fiftieth anniversary, its manufacturer presented gold-plated rolls to both Wagga and Bendigo—a fittingly shared memorial to a famously disputed snack.
